alignment.note: Greek εὐθὺς ('immediately') is rendered adverbially in Latin by confestim, but the Peshitta employs the temporal idiom ܘܒܪ ܫܥܬܗ ('and in that very hour/moment'), a two-word periphrastic construction typical of Syriac for marking immediacy.

Greek uses the neuter diminutive τὸ κοράσιον with the definite article; the Peshitta ܛܠܝܬܐ and Latin puella both render the noun without an explicit article (Syriac uses the emphatic state, Latin lacks articles), so the definiteness is conveyed structurally rather than lexically.

Greek imperfect περιεπάτει ('was walking') is matched by Latin imperfect ambulabat; the Peshitta expresses durative aspect periphrastically with the participle ܡܗܠܟܐ plus the auxiliary ܗܘܬ, the standard Syriac means of forming the past continuous.

Greek imperfect ἦν ('she was') and Latin erat are single finite verbs; the Peshitta uses the existential predicate ܐܝܬܝܗ with the auxiliary ܗܘܬ, a periphrastic construction rendering the same copulative sense.

Greek ἐτῶν δώδεκα ('of twelve years') and Latin annorum render age as a simple genitive of years; the Peshitta uses the idiom ܒܪܬ ܫܢܝܢ ('daughter of years'), the standard Semitic construction for stating age, requiring the construct noun ܒܪܬ.
The Clementine Vulgate inserts a colon after duodecim to mark the syntactic break before the concluding clause; Greek and Syriac mark this boundary with the conjunction alone.
Greek aorist ἐξέστησαν and Latin perfect obstupuerunt are simple finite verbs; the Peshitta uses the participle ܡܬܕܡܪܝܢ with the auxiliary ܗܘܘ, a periphrastic past expressing the onset of amazement.

The Greek attests a second εὐθὺς ('immediately') qualifying the amazement, a characteristically Markan repetition of the adverb; neither the Peshitta nor the Vulgate transmits this second occurrence, smoothing the redundancy.
